question:
[MCQ] Based on the video clip, what probe orientation is being used at the start of the scan, and what is the acquisition objective?
A. Transverse plane; begin at the superior portion to start a full-volume sweep
B. Longitudinal (sagittal) plane; start at the midline to obtain a standard 2D survey sweep of the target organ.
C. Oblique plane; begin at the inferior margin to locate the landmark anatomy before sweeping superiorly for partial coverage.
D. Transverse plane; center the structure of interest to optimize depth and focus before acquiring representative still images rather than a full-volume sweep.
groundtruth: The operator places the probe in a transverse orientation high on the right liver lobe to start the protocol from the superior aspect before sweeping through the liver.
original_question:

B. Longitudinal (sagittal) plane; start at the midline to obtain a standard 2D survey sweep of the target organ.
C. Transverse plane; center the structure of interest to optimize depth and focus before acquiring representative still images rather than a full-volume sweep.
D. Oblique plane; begin at the inferior margin to locate the landmark anatomy before sweeping superiorly for partial coverage.

inference_metadata.raw_response:
Answer: A
First, the on-screen label explicitly states "TRANS RIGHT LIVER", confirming the transverse scan plane, so options B (longitudinal) and C (oblique) are incorrect. The clip shows the probe performing a continuous sweep of the right liver starting at the superior diaphragmatic margin, consistent with a full-volume sweep, eliminating option D which refers to acquiring still images rather than a sweep.

question:
[MCQ] Based on the video clip, what physical technique change is shown, and what is the main reason for doing it?
A. Switching to an intercostal scanning window; to reduce rib shadowing and improve visualization of the target area.
B. Changing transducer grip/hand position; to better reach and visualize the lateral boundary ergonomically
C. Applying graded compression with the probe; to assess compressibility and differentiate bowel or vein from a noncompressible structure.
D. Rotating the transducer 90° into a longitudinal view; to confirm the structure’s course in an orthogonal plane.
groundtruth: The operator changes grip on the transducer to improve ergonomics and enable effective visualization of the lateral border.

inference_metadata.raw_response:
Answer: A
Explanation: The examination is of the right liver, where subcostal scanning often produces rib shadowing that obscures visualization of liver parenchyma. Switching to an intercostal window between rib spaces eliminates these shadow artifacts, allowing clearer imaging of the targeted right liver tissue.

question:

question:
[MCQ] Based on the video clip, what coverage strategy is demonstrated, and why is it used?
A. Fanning (rocking) the probe through the organ while keeping it in view; used to sample different insonation angles and reduce anisotropy rather than to ensure lateral edge coverage.
B. Cranial-to-caudal sweep along the long axis without leaving the organ; used to assess superior–inferior extent and look for focal lesions rather than to avoid missing edge anatomy.
C. Sliding the probe slightly medially with lighter pressure; used to optimize an intercostal window and reduce rib shadowing, not to interrogate the far lateral margin.
D. Lateral sweep fully out of the organ with added pressure, then return to the landmark; ensures complete lateral coverage and avoids missed edge anatomy
groundtruth: The operator sweeps laterally with firm pressure until fully out of the liver, then sweeps back medially to the IVC, completing coverage of the superior right lobe from the IVC to the lateral edge and back.

inference_metadata.raw_response:

The video shows a lateral sweep that moves the probe fully out of the liver (evidenced by the dark segment with only rib shadowing visible when the organ is no longer in view) before returning to the original liver landmark. This strategy ensures complete coverage of the lateral edge of the liver, so no pathology or anatomy at the far lateral margin is missed.
